subject: Business
title: Quantitative Easing: Printing Digital Money
description: One-minute skill: Quantitative Easing: Printing Digital Money.

hook.text: After 2008, the Fed created $4.5 trillion out of thin air. No printing presses. Just keystrokes.

buildup.text: Quantitative easing (QE) means the central bank buys government bonds to inject money into the financial system.

discovery.text: QE pushed interest rates near zero and flooded markets with liquidity, propping up asset prices.

twist.text: Critics say QE inflated stocks and real estate — helping the wealthy while leaving wages flat for everyone else.

climax.text: During COVID, the Fed added another $5 trillion. Total US money supply roughly doubled in two years.

punchline.text: Money creation is now a keyboard shortcut.

quiz.question: What is quantitative easing?
options: A central bank buying bonds to inject money into the economy
A government program to reduce spending

details.summary: Quantitative easing is a central bank policy of creating new money electronically to purchase government bonds and other assets from the financial system. It aims to lower long-term interest rates and stimulate lending when conventional rate cuts have reached their lower limit.
details.whyItMatters: QE became the dominant crisis tool after 2008 and during COVID-19, injecting trillions into economies. Understanding QE explains why asset prices surged, savings yields collapsed, and debates about inflation and inequality intensified.
takeaways: Central banks create new digital money to buy bonds and financial assets
QE lowers long-term interest rates when short-term rates are already near zero
Critics argue QE inflates asset prices and widens wealth inequality

faq.question: Is quantitative easing the same as printing money?
faq.answer: Not exactly. QE creates digital reserves that banks hold at the central bank. These reserves do not directly enter the real economy unless banks lend them out. However, QE expands the monetary base and can contribute to inflation if it fuels excessive lending.

faq.question: Why does QE tend to increase wealth inequality?
faq.answer: QE primarily boosts prices of assets like stocks, bonds, and real estate. People who own these assets see their wealth rise, while those without investments see little benefit. Wages and savings account returns remain depressed, widening the gap between asset owners and workers.
